findings.title: Error handling should include clean-up
findings.description: The vulnerability lies in the error handling mechanism within the entrypoint function, where errors are printed but not properly handled or cleaned up. The root cause is the lack of structured error management—only `error.print()` is called before returning the error, with no attempt to release resources or revert state changes that may have occurred before the error. An attacker could potentially trigger error conditions repeatedly to cause resource exhaustion or leave the program in an inconsistent state, although direct exploitation for fund theft is unlikely. The impact is primarily on system maintainability and observability, as errors may go unnoticed or unlogged in production environments, making debugging and monitoring difficult.

findings.title: More error types to be more granular and informative
findings.description: The contract defines only a single error type (`InvalidInstruction`) in the `VestingError` enum, which limits the ability to distinguish between different failure modes. This lack of granularity stems from incomplete error modeling during development. While this does not directly enable exploitation, it hampers debugging and monitoring, as callers and off-chain systems cannot determine the specific cause of a failure. An attacker could potentially exploit ambiguous error responses to probe the system without triggering specific alerts. The impact is reduced operational visibility and delayed response to potential issues, increasing the overall attack surface over time.

findings.title: Use constants to safeguard against unwanted future changes
findings.description: Hardcoded seed arrays and configuration values (e.g., seeds of type [u8; 32] and `number_of_schedules: u32`) are used directly in the code without being defined as constants. This practice increases the risk of inconsistencies during future code modifications, as the same value may be duplicated across multiple locations and could be altered in one place but not another. The root cause is poor code hygiene and lack of abstraction for fixed parameters. If a developer updates one instance of a magic value but misses others, it could lead to incorrect account derivations or state mismatches. The impact is potential logic errors or denial of service due to invalid account validations, especially during upgrades or forks.
